title: Detection of Drive-by Target
summary: This detection strategy covers the drive by target step, where an adversary prepares a website that compromises visitors and then sends traffic to it, usually by injecting a redirect into a legitimate but weakly maintained site, by buying an expired domain, or by hosting a page that checks the visitor before delivering an exploit. It matters because the preparation is silent, so the practical detection sits on the victim side: proxy and network logs showing a small number of users redirected through a chain of unrelated hosts to a page that serves script, intrusion detection alerts for exploit delivery, endpoint records of browser or plug in child processes, and domain monitoring for newly registered or recently re-registered lookalike sites. The telemetry that makes it possible is secure web gateway records with referrer chains, domain name system resolver logs, endpoint detection and response process trees, and intrusion detection signatures for known exploit kits. Detection fails because legitimate advertising and content networks redirect users constantly, and because the exploit page often serves harmless content to the wrong visitor.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for a website that is set up to harm its visitors. The attacker places the trap first and sends people to it later. The rule watches for users who pass through several odd redirects to one page. It also watches for office programs or browsers starting unusual child processes.
beginner.whyItMatters: The visitor needs to do nothing except open the page. There is no attachment to inspect in advance. You cannot see the trap from the outside, so you must watch what happens to your users. Early warning lets you block the domain and check which devices were affected.
howItWorks: The web gateway records each request with the address, the referrer and the full page path.
Redirect chains are rebuilt from those records, so a user path through several unrelated sites becomes visible.
Resolver logs show first time lookups of newly registered domains from corporate devices.
Endpoint detection records process trees. A browser or document reader that starts a script host is unusual.
The rule selects users who reached a low reputation page after many redirects. It also selects a browser that started a child process.
Matching devices are isolated for review, and the domains are added to the block list.
beginner.example: Think of a footpath where someone has loosened one paving stone. Nothing looks wrong until a walker steps on it. The person who loosened the stone never returns to the path. This detection checks the ankles of the walkers, not the stone.
takeaways: Compromised visitors are the only reliable signal, because the trap sits outside your control.
A long redirect chain through unrelated domains is a strong warning sign.
A browser or document reader that starts a script host is worth an immediate look.

objectives: Explain how a drive by target page differs from a phishing message.
Identify the proxy, resolver and endpoint records that reveal a drive by visit.
Write a rule that combines redirect chain length with domain age and process behaviour.
Describe how to isolate a device that may have run exploit code.
Explain how domain monitoring supports blocking before users are sent to the page.
dataSources: Secure web gateway logs with requested address, referrer chain, user agent and page path per user
Domain name system resolver logs showing first time lookups of newly registered or recently re-registered domains
Endpoint detection and response process creation records showing browser and document reader child processes
Intrusion detection and prevention alerts for exploit kit traffic patterns and known exploit signatures
Web server and content delivery logs for corporate sites showing injected scripts or unexpected redirect rules
logic: The pattern is a corporate user reaching a low reputation or newly registered page through a redirect chain that crosses several unrelated domains, combined with either a script host process started by a browser or document reader, or an intrusion detection alert for exploit delivery in the same session. The fields that must be correlated are the user and device, the redirect chain and its length, the age and reputation of the final domain, the user agent and plug in version, the process tree on the endpoint, and any subsequent outbound connection to a new address from the same device. The benign case is advertising and content networks that redirect through tracking domains to a video or article, where the process tree stays clean; the malicious case is a referral from a legitimate but compromised site to a page that runs browser version checks, delivers encoded script, and is followed within seconds by a new process on the endpoint or a new outbound connection.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Long Redirect Chain to New Domain With Script Host Child Process
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: web_proxy
# detection:
#   selection_web:
#     url_reputation: 'low'
#     domain_age_days: < 30
#     redirect_chain_length: > 3
#   selection_endpoint:
#     parent_image|endswith:
#       - 'browser.exe'
#       - 'document-reader.exe'
#     image|endswith:
#       - 'script-host.exe'
#   condition: selection_web or selection_endpoint
# level: high
falsePositives: Advertising and affiliate networks that route a click through several tracking domains before the article loads
Email marketing links that pass through a click tracker and a shortener before reaching a partner site
Content delivery networks that serve a page from a newly created edge hostname after a site relaunch
A browser extension or document reader component that starts a script host for a legitimate internal application
tuningNotes: Allow list the tracking and shortener domains your marketing and business partners use, and set the redirect chain threshold above the longest chain those produce. Scope the process rule to script hosts that are not started by approved business applications, and keep a list of those applications up to date. Require either the low reputation final domain or the process evidence before raising severity, so a long chain alone stays a low severity record. Because a careful adversary sends traffic only to visitors from the target country or network, add a monthly review of newly registered domains resolved by corporate devices and check any that later appear in proxy or endpoint telemetry.
